title: Cognitive Biases You Should Know
description: Common thinking traps that skew judgment and decisions, each with a plain-language explanation so you can spot them in everyday life.
subject: social-sciences

cards.definition: Tendency to seek out, favor, and remember information that supports what you already believe.
Sticking with something because of what you've already put into it, rather than judging it on its future value.
Drawing conclusions only from the successes that remain visible while overlooking the failures that dropped out of view.
Relying too heavily on the first piece of information you encounter, such as an opening price, when making a judgment.
Judging how likely or common something is by how easily examples come to mind.
Tendency for people with limited skill in an area to overestimate their own competence.
Believing after an event that you knew all along it would happen.
Overemphasizing personality and underestimating the situation when explaining other people's behavior.
Crediting your successes to your own abilities while blaming your failures on outside factors.
Adopting a belief or behavior because many other people have already adopted it.
Letting one positive trait, such as attractiveness, shape your overall impression of a person.
Feeling the pain of a loss more strongly than the pleasure of an equivalent gain.
Reacting differently to the same information depending on how it's presented, such as "90% survive" versus "10% die."
Believing past random outcomes change the odds of future independent ones, like expecting heads after a run of tails.
Preferring that things stay the same, even when a change would likely leave you better off.
Giving more weight and attention to negative experiences or information than to equally strong positive ones.
Believing you are less likely than other people to experience bad outcomes.
Underestimating how much time, money, or effort a future task will take, even when similar tasks have run over before.
Overestimating how much other people notice your appearance or behavior.
Difficulty imagining what it's like not to know something you already know, which makes explaining it to beginners harder.
Favoring members of your own group over people outside it.
Valuing something more highly simply because you own it.
Overestimating how much other people share your opinions, beliefs, and habits.
